projectDetail:
An unreleased multiplayer title currently in development. The game has not been announced, so its setting, mechanics and release plans are held back here. What can be said is where my work on it sits: the runtime architecture the gameplay work is built on, the simulation that drives non-player characters and their navigation, and the internal tooling the team tests against. It is built with Rojo and Luau on a Knit service and controller architecture with a Roact and Rodux UI layer.

Happy to talk through the engineering side of this one in more detail in person, within what I am able to share.
myContribution:
1. Established the project's technical foundation: structured the codebase into per-system modules and wrote the internal technical documentation the team develops against.
2. Designed and built the character simulation framework: a single agent runtime driven by swappable, self-registering behaviour modules, with character types defined as shared read-only configuration rather than branching code.
3. Built the perception layer that decides what each agent can see and respond to, including true line-of-sight checks and shared target selection.
4. Replaced the engine's built-in pathfinding with a custom navigation stack: a walkability grid rasterised from raycasts, a synchronous A* search with corner-cut prevention and path smoothing, and a crowd avoidance layer.
5. Built the agent spawning pipeline, including placement rules, model-driven rigs, animation and whole-map population passes.
6. Adapted several systems I had already hardened on a shipped title so the project had a working, testable shell early in pre-production.
7. Built the internal developer tooling the rest of the team tests against: a spawn harness, navigation and sensor debug overlays, and runtime state readouts.
engine: Roblox Studio, Luau (Rojo, Knit, Roact, Rodux)

additionalDetails.title: Custom Navigation in Place of the Engine's Pathfinder
additionalDetails.description: Characters were walking straight into level geometry. Several causes stacked up: no navigation layer at all beneath the behaviour logic, corner-cutting from a waypoint radius set too wide, line-of-sight rays that terminated inside the target's own body, and a slope limit permissive enough that agents climbed obstacles instead of walking around them. The structural cause was that the engine's navmesh disagreed with what a raycast actually hits - geometry omitted by collision fidelity, surfaces treated as walkable floor that were not, and a single global agent radius that could not be simultaneously narrow enough for tight gaps and wide enough for the largest character. Navigation was rebuilt on a grid rasterised from raycasts, so it cannot disagree with physics because raycasts are what build it, searched by a synchronous eight-way A* that forbids diagonals through corner gaps and smooths the result. Clearance became per-character-type and requested at search time, which is what a global agent radius should have been. Because the search is synchronous, an entire category of scaffolding that existed only to survive an asynchronous pathfinder disappeared - the request queue, generation guard, straight-line fallback, failure counter, back-off and route truncation - cutting the movement agent to a third of its size, while local look-ahead and stuck detection were kept for the things a static grid genuinely cannot see, such as another agent or a door that just closed.

projectDetail: "Clean-a-Crime" is a live Roblox multiplayer game where a crew of players is hired to erase the evidence left behind after a heist. Teams pick a map and difficulty from the lobby, drop into a crime scene, and work against the clock to scrub bloodstains, grab and grind up evidence and bodies, unlock sealed rooms and the vault by hacking scattered control panels, rearrange disturbed objects back into place, and capture and extract hostages before the job is called in. The game runs a full live-service loop on top of that core: maps and difficulties unlock by level, cash and XP feed equipment and stat upgrades, and the economy is driven by gamepasses, developer products, limited starter and VIP offers, daily rewards, daily tasks, a spin wheel, referrals and leaderboards. Seasonal events such as the Clown, Ghost, Rainbow and Glitch events swap in event maps and event-only objectives. It is built with Rojo and Luau on a Knit service and controller architecture with a Roact and Rodux UI layer.
myContribution:
1. Built the core grab, carry and drop system including client-authoritative grabbing for responsiveness, ghost placement preview, wall awareness, drop validation, carry stack limits and full PC, mobile and gamepad support.
2. Built the grinder and disposal loop that converts collected evidence into payout, along with its zone, effects and visual handling.
3. Designed and implemented the door unlock system: procedurally spawned hacking panels, multi-panel vault doors, and placement rules that keep every run solvable.
4. Implemented the hostage capture objective end to end, from spawner and rope-constrained dragging to animations and delivery zones.
5. Implemented the rearrange-object objective and the generator objective, including their spawners, task templates and client controllers.
6. Owned the mission flow: refactored the mission service, extracted its logic layers, added the exit handler and built the animated mission summary screen.
7. Owned the lobby: host panel, map and difficulty selection with level gating, map unlocks, teleport flow, the party system through two revisions and party reward boosts.
8. Built the equipment system with its shop, tier previews, equip flow and upgrade progression, plus the stat upgrade panels.
9. Built the monetization layer: gamepasses, developer products, pack purchases, limited-time starter and VIP offers, the premium shop, and a centralized product registry so every storefront grants through one audited path.
10. Built the retention systems: seven-day daily rewards with offline grants, the daily task system, free chests, the spin wheel, social media rewards and the referral system.
11. Built live event content and systems including the Clown event and the seasonal event maps and event-only objectives.
12. Wrote an object-oriented input system with rebindable actions and console support, and a shared UI toolkit (toasts, global alerts, panel stack, responsive scaling) used across the Roact and Rodux front end.
13. Instrumented the game with custom analytics and funnel events for lobby, tutorial, map selection and interaction failures.
engine: Roblox Studio, Luau (Rojo, Knit, Roact, Rodux)

additionalDetails.title: Procedural Door Unlock & Panel Placement
additionalDetails.description: Sealed rooms and the vault are opened by hacking control panels that are scattered across the map at mission start rather than placed by hand. Each run spawns five panels across authored spawn points, with the vault door requiring two of them, so no two sessions play the same way. The hard part was the placement rules: a panel must never be locked inside the very room that the same panel unlocks, only a limited number of panels may sit inside locked rooms at all, and each locked room can hold at most one. Spawn points carry metadata for which room they belong to, whether that room is locked, and how near or far they sit from a given door, and the spawner treats distance as a preference but the solvability rules as hard constraints. The result is a layout that is randomized every run but can never soft-lock the team.

additionalDetails.title: Grab & Carry Under Network Latency
additionalDetails.description: Grabbing, carrying and dropping physical objects is the moment-to-moment verb of the whole game, so it had to feel instant while still being validated by the server. The system runs the grab locally on the client for immediate feedback, shows a ghost preview of where the object will land, and reconciles with a server-side grab service that owns the authoritative state. Getting this right meant solving a long list of physical edge cases: grab point offsets on irregular meshes, bodies resting vertically against walls, objects re-entering the grab state mid-grind, releases into disposal zones, and hidden geometry that could be triggered through a wall. Carry capacity itself later became a monetization surface, with a purchasable stack limit and auto-consumed boosters layered on top of the same system.

additionalDetails.title: Live-Service Economy at Scale
additionalDetails.description: The game earns through gamepasses, developer products, limited-time offers and packs, spread across several storefronts that all had to agree with each other. Purchase awarding was centralized behind a shared product registry and price fetcher, so every surface reads the same catalogue and grants through a single audited path rather than each panel implementing its own. On top of that sits the reliability work that a real-money loop needs but players never see: reconciling entitlements for sessions that ended mid-transaction, anchoring every timed offer and reward streak to authoritative server time rather than the device clock, and granting rewards accrued while a player was offline on their next login. Most of the effort in this area went into the failure paths, not the happy path.

projectDetail: "Block Tiles Earn Cyrpto" is a blockchain-integrated game inspired by classic block-stacking gameplay. Players are rewarded with virtual currency based on the number of lines they clear during gameplay. Once users accumulate enough currency, they can request real-world payouts directly to their Binance or Coinbase account. This system incentivizes skillful play while integrating a real-money reward mechanism.
myContribution:
1. Implemented multiple authentication options including Email, Facebook, Google, and Guest login.
2. Integrated PlayFab backend for account management, economy, and data handling.
3. Added AdMob monetization including Banner, Interstitial, Rewarded, and App Open Ads.
4. Developed Binance withdrawal functionality for crypto payouts.
5. Strengthened security to prevent exploits and cheating behaviors.
6. Provided live support to players with login and account-related issues.
7. Diagnosed and resolved gameplay and system bugs across devices.

additionalDetails.title: Reward System & Payout Mechanism
additionalDetails.description: One of the key challenges was implementing a reward structure that balanced engaging gameplay with real-world payouts. Users were awarded virtual currency upon completing levels based on difficulty. Once they reached the withdrawal threshold, they could request payment to their Binance or Coinbase accounts by submitting their email. Ensuring this system was seamless, secure, and abuse-proof required thoughtful design and ongoing refinement.

additionalDetails.title: Exploits & Fair Play
additionalDetails.description: As the game involved real monetary value, preventing unfair advantages was critical. One notable exploit involved users manipulating their device's local time to bypass the withdrawal cooldown period. To counter this, we integrated PlayFab's trusted server time to validate all withdrawal timing and enforce cooldowns reliably. Users attempting to bypass this mechanism were automatically flagged and temporarily banned. Ongoing monitoring and backend-side validation helped maintain a fair and cheat-free environment.

projectDetail: "Minesweeper Earn Crypto" is a blockchain-integrated casual game inspired by the classic Minesweeper gameplay. Players could choose from three difficulty levels — Easy, Medium, and Hard — and were awarded virtual currency upon successfully clearing each round. The reward amount varied depending on the selected difficulty. Once players accumulated enough virtual currency, they could initiate a withdrawal by providing their Binance or Coinbase email address, allowing them to receive crypto payouts directly to their exchange wallets. The game blended nostalgic gameplay with real-world incentives, encouraging both strategy and engagement.

projectDetail: A custom inventory and order management app designed to streamline operations across two family-run businesses — a tiles and sanitary dealership, and a wall paint store. The system adapts to the unique workflows and measurement units of each showroom, ensuring accurate stock, order, and role-based access management.
myContribution:
1. Developed custom login with access-level-based dashboards.
2. Implemented dual-unit product ordering (sft/carton vs. pieces).
3. Integrated Google Sheets import for bulk stock entry.
4. Developed dynamic UI to separate tiles and paint showroom workflows.
5. Handled inventory, order, and user account management.

additionalDetails.title: Complex Unit Handling
additionalDetails.description: Each product followed a different measurement standard — such as square feet, cartons, pieces, grams, or liters. The system had to intelligently identify and adapt to each type for accurate stock tracking and billing.

additionalDetails.title: PDF Invoice Generation Without Unity SDK
additionalDetails.description: I used Unity 3D to develop my app because I am a game developer and not familiar with other app frameworks. Since there is no PDF generator SDK in Unity, I had to use a .NET PDF library to create invoice PDF files directly from the Unity app.

additionalDetails.title: High-Stakes Validation Challenges
additionalDetails.description: Accurate calculations were critical. A small logic or validation issue could lead to discrepancies in billing, risking business credibility. Rapid debugging and issue resolution were essential to maintain trust with customers.
